questions.tag: Case study: basicity, acylation and diazonium salts
questions.question:
Amines form salts with mineral acids. Basicity depends on structure, and primary and secondary amines undergo acylation. Hinsberg’s test distinguishes amine classes. Aryldiazonium compounds allow replacement of the diazonium group.
(a)(i) Why is methylamine a stronger aqueous base than trimethylamine? (ii) Identify A and B in CH₃CONH₂ → A (NaOBr) → B (C₆H₅COCl/base). [2]
(b) A C₃H₉N amine gives an alkali-insoluble product in the Hinsberg test. Identify it. OR Convert aniline to benzonitrile. [1]
(c) Why acetylate aniline before nitrating it? [1]
questions.solution:
(a)(i) Methyl-group induction favours basicity, but trimethylammonium is less effectively hydrated because of steric crowding. The balance in water favours methylamine [1]. (ii) A = CH₃NH₂ by Hofmann bromamide degradation [½]. B = C₆H₅CONHCH₃ by benzoylation [½].
(b) CH₃CH₂NHCH₃, N-methylethanamine [1]. OR diazotise aniline with NaNO₂/HCl at 0–5 °C, then use CuCN to obtain C₆H₅CN [1].
(c) Acetylation moderates ring activation and favours the para nitro derivative. It also reduces formation of the meta-directing anilinium ion [1].

questions.tag: Case study: crystal-field splitting and magnetic behaviour
questions.question:
VBT describes geometry and magnetic behaviour. In CFT, ligands lift d-orbital degeneracy. Field strength affects electron pairing.
(a) Which orbitals rise in energy when octahedral ligands approach, and why? [2]
(b) Give the CFT configurations of Co in [CoF₆]³⁻ and [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺. [1]
(c) Why is tetrahedral [NiCl₄]²⁻ paramagnetic while tetrahedral [Ni(CO)₄] is diamagnetic? OR State the hybridisation and magnetism of [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻. [1]
questions.solution:
(a) dx²−y² and dz² form the higher eg set [1]. Their lobes point along the axes towards the ligands, increasing repulsion [1].
(b) Both contain Co³⁺ (3d⁶). F⁻ gives high-spin t2g⁴eg² [½]. NH₃ gives low-spin t2g⁶eg⁰ [½].
(c) Weak-field Cl⁻ leaves two unpaired electrons on Ni²⁺ (d⁸) [½]. Ni in [Ni(CO)₄] is formally Ni(0), d¹⁰, with all electrons paired [½]. OR [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ is low-spin d⁵, t2g⁵, with d²sp³ hybridisation and one unpaired electron [½ + ½].

questions.question:
(a)(i) E°(M²⁺/M) values in V: V −1.18, Cr −0.91, Mn −1.18, Fe −0.44, Co −0.28, Ni −0.25, Cu +0.34. Explain (I) irregular variation, (II) Cu’s positive value and (III) Mn’s strongly negative value. [3]
(ii) Write balanced ionic equations for oxidation of iodide by permanganate in acidic and alkaline media. [2]
OR

questions.solution:
(a)(i)(I) Atomisation and ionisation enthalpies vary irregularly along the series, along with hydration contributions [1]. (II) Cu has high atomisation enthalpy and its hydration enthalpy does not compensate for the energy needed to form Cu²⁺(aq) [1]. (III) Mn²⁺ is stabilised by half-filled 3d⁵ [1].
(ii) Acid: 2MnO₄⁻ + 10I⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5I₂ + 8H₂O [1]. Alkaline: 2MnO₄⁻ + I⁻ + H₂O → 2MnO₂ + IO₃⁻ + 2OH⁻ [1].
(b)(i) Ce (+4) and Eu or Yb (+2) [½ + ½]. (ii) Variable oxidation states and intermediate formation can provide lower-energy pathways [1]. (iii) Chromium has stronger interatomic metallic bonding, with more electrons available from (n−1)d and ns orbitals [1]. (iv) 4MnO₄⁻ + 4H⁺ → 4MnO₂ + 3O₂ + 2H₂O [1]. This is a redox reaction [1].

questions.question:
(a) At 298 K find E and ΔG for Mg(s) | Mg²⁺(0.01 M) || Ag⁺(0.001 M) | Ag(s). E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = −2.37 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. Use F = 96,500 C mol⁻¹.
OR
(b) At 25 °C find E for 2AgCl(s) + H₂(g, 0.4 atm) → 2Ag(s) + 2H⁺(0.1 M) + 2Cl⁻(0.2 M). ΔG° = −43,500 J mol⁻¹. Use F = 96,500 C mol⁻¹.
questions.solution:
(a) Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag, n = 2. E° = 0.80 − (−2.37) = 3.17 V. Q = 0.01/(0.001)² = 10⁴. Nernst equation [1], substitution of concentrations and E° [1], E = 3.17 − (0.0591/2) log(10⁴) ≈ 3.052 V [1]. ΔG = −nFE [½]; substitute n = 2, F = 96,500 and E ≈ 3.052 V [½]; ΔG ≈ −589 kJ mol⁻¹ [1].
(b) n = 2. Use ΔG° = −nFE° [½]. Substitute the given ΔG° and nF [1] to get E° = 43,500/(2 × 96,500) ≈ 0.225 V [½]. Write E = E° − (0.059/2) log Q [1], with Q ≈ (0.1)²(0.2)²/0.4 = 10⁻³ [1]. Using the scheme’s rounded values gives E = 0.225 + 0.0885 = 0.3135 V [1].

questions.questionSearchText: Osmosis is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low solute concentration to a solution of high solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood’s osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar. questions.questionSearchText: Like NH3, nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore sp3 hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order 1º > 2º > 3º. It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc. (a) Complete the following equations : 2 (i) LiAlH4 (i) CH3CONH2 —————→ (ii) H2O Fe + HCl (ii) ————→ (b) Why primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines ? 1 (c) Classify the following amines as primary, secondary or tertiary : 1 (i) (ii) OR (c) Out of Butan–1–amine and Butan–1–ol, which is more soluble in water ? 1

questions.questionSearchText: Like NH3, nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore sp3 hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order 1º > 2º > 3º. It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc. (a) Complete the following equations : 2 (i) LiAlH4 (i) CH3CONH2 —————→ (ii) H2O Fe + HCl (ii) ————→ (b) Why primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines ? 1 (c) Classify the following amines as primary, secondary or tertiary : 1 (i) (ii) OR (c) Out of Butan–1–amine and Butan–1–ol, which is more soluble in water ? 1

questions.questionSearchText: Osmosis is a process by which the molecules of a solvent pass from a solution of low solute concentration to a solution of high solute concentration through a semi-permeable membrane. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property. When the applied pressure on a solution exceeds its osmotic pressure, reverse osmosis occurs. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood’s osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar. When two solutions are separated by a semipermeable membrane and they have same osmotic pressure they are said to be isotonic. Of the two solutions separated by a semipermeable membrane, if one is a lower osmotic pressure, it is said to be hypotonic relative to the second solution. If it has a higher osmotic pressure, than the second solution, it is said to be hypertonic relative to the second solution. The osmotic pressure associated with the fluid inside the blood cell is equivalent to that of 0.9% (mass/volume) sodium chloride solution called normal saline solution and it is safe to inject intravenously. Osmotic pressure is vital in daily life and nature. It helps in explain, why IV fluids match blood’s osmotic pressure, its also the principle behind food preservation using salt or sugar. (a) Calculate the amount of CaCl2 (i = 2.59) dissolved in 2.46 litre of water such that its osmotic pressure is 0.70 atm at 27°C. [Given : R = 0.082 L atm K–1 mol–1, molar mass of CaCl2 = 111 g mol–1] 2 (b) When raisins are kept in water, they get swollen. Name the phenomenon involved in this process. 1 OR (b) Why osmotic pressure is more advantageous than other colligative properties ? 1 (c) Which phenomenon is responsible for desalination of sea water ? 1

questions.questionSearchText: Like NH3, nitrogen atom of amine is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons. Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore sp3 hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal. Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water due to the formation of hydrogen bond with water molecules. The solubility decreases as the molar mass of amines increases due to increase in size of hydrophobic part. Higher amines are insoluble in water. However amines are less soluble in water than alcohols because of low electronegativity of nitrogen as compared to oxygen. Boiling points of isomeric amines follow the order 1º > 2º > 3º. It is due to the fact the amines are held together due to hydrogen bonding. Extent of hydrogen bonding is more in primary amines than in secondary amines as two hydrogen atoms are available for hydrogen bond formation. Tertiary amines do not show hydrogen bonding because of the absence of hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen. Amines can be prepared from, nitro compounds, nitriles, amides etc. (a) Complete the following equations : 2 (i) LiAlH4 (i) CH3CONH2 —————→ (ii) H2O Fe + HCl (ii) ————→ (b) Why primary amines have higher boiling points than tertiary amines ? 1 (c) Classify the following amines as primary, secondary or tertiary : 1 (i) (ii) OR (c) Out of Butan–1–amine and Butan–1–ol, which is more soluble in water ? 1

questions.questionSearchText: 30. Electrochemistry is the study of the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy. Many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy. In electrolysis, electrical energy is converted directly into chemical energy. The product of an electrolytic reaction depends on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrode used. Oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potential too, affect the products of electrolysis. Electrolysis plays an important role in most people’s daily lives, whether it is for the manufacturing of aluminium, electroplating of metals, or the synthesis of chemical compounds. Michael Faraday was the first scientist who proposed two laws to explain the quantitative aspects of electrolysis, popularly known as Faraday’s laws of electrolysis. Faraday’s laws of electrolysis provide a basis for mathematical analysis of the mass deposited at electrodes and the amount of charge passed through them. Faraday’s laws are fundamental in various applications, including electroplating, metal extraction, battery technology and chemical synthesis. These laws also help in environmental monitoring and in various chemistry experiments. Answer the following questions : (a) Predict the products of electrolysis in each of the following : 2 (i) An aqueous solution of CuCl2 with platinum electrodes. (ii) A concentrated solution of H2SO4 with platinum electrodes. questions.questionSearchText: 29. Electrochemistry is the study of the relationship between chemical energy and electrical energy. Many spontaneously occurring chemical reactions liberate electrical energy. In electrolysis, electrical energy is converted directly into chemical energy. The product of an electrolytic reaction depends on the nature of the material being electrolysed and the type of electrode used. Oxidising and reducing species present in the electrolytic cell and their standard electrode potential too, affect the products of electrolysis. Electrolysis plays an important role in most people’s daily lives, whether it is for the manufacturing of aluminium, electroplating of metals, or the synthesis of chemical compounds. Michael Faraday was the first scientist who proposed two laws to explain the quantitative aspects of electrolysis, popularly known as Faraday’s laws of electrolysis. Faraday’s laws of electrolysis provide a basis for mathematical analysis of the mass deposited at electrodes and the amount of charge passed through them. Faraday’s laws are fundamental in various applications, including electroplating, metal extraction, battery technology and chemical synthesis. These laws also help in environmental monitoring and in various chemistry experiments. questions.questionSearchText: 30. Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or molecules that provide such units on hydrolysis. They are broadly classified into three groups : monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. Monosaccharide units are held together by glycosidic linkages to form disaccharides or polysaccharides. Starch and cellulose are polysaccharides. Starch is a polymer of α-glucose and consists of two components : Amylose and Amylopectin. Amylose is water soluble, having 15 – 20% of starch, whereas Amylopectin is insoluble in water, having 80 – 85% starch. Chemically, amylose is a long unbranched chain of α-glucose units held together by C1 − C4 glycosidic linkage. Amylopectin is a branched chain of α-glucose units held together by C1 − C4 and C1 − C6 glycosidic linkages.
